title: Zephyrine and the Well
premise: Gideon Brightwater, a small-town pest controller, is hired to deal with something living in the walls of a farmhouse that leaves human fingerprints in the dust. When his childhood imaginary friend Zephyrine appears on his porch — unchanged after forty years — she is drawn into the haunting, because she is the thing that was taken in 1974: a real girl, unaged, stolen from time itself. To survive, Gideon must return her to the well on the property where she vanished, knowing that doing so will erase every memory anyone has of her, including his own. In the end he pays that price: the farmhouse goes quiet, and Gideon wakes with a life that has a hole in it shaped like a friend he can no longer name.
about_author: August Ravensworth is the pen name of a former rural insurance adjuster who spent years inspecting abandoned farmhouses across the Midwest. Their fiction draws on case files, local legends, and the unsettling habit old houses have of keeping records.

chapters.title: Fingerprints in the Dust
chapters.summary: Gideon Brightwater, pest controller, takes a call from the Hollis farm: something in the walls, and small fingerprints in the dust where no child has lived since 1974. Told in Gideon's pragmatic POV, he keeps the lights on and counts the doors — eleven, then twelve. The beat is professional calm beginning to crack.

chapters.title: The Counting House
chapters.summary: Gideon returns at dawn to verify his count and finds thirteen doors in a nine-room farmhouse. The Hollis widow, Ruth, admits the house 'grows rooms' every autumn, and that her husband stopped sleeping in 1974. POV alternates to Ruth's diary entries. The emotional beat is the slow dread of a house that keeps books.

chapters.title: Zephyrine
chapters.summary: On his porch at home, Gideon finds a girl of about nine, dry as paper, wearing a 1970s corduroy coat: Zephyrine, the imaginary friend he invented at age six and outgrew at seven. She is unchanged, and she knows his name. His POV; the beat is vertigo — the past standing on his welcome mat, asking to come in.

chapters.title: What Imaginary Means
chapters.summary: Zephyrine stays in Gideon's spare room, sleeping standing up, leaving no heat signature. He tests her — mirrors, photographs, salt — and she fails every test except the one that matters: she remembers his childhood better than he does. His POV with mounting tenderness and fear. The beat: you cannot unlove someone by declaring them unreal.

chapters.title: The Well on Hollis Land
chapters.summary: Ruth shows Gideon the capped well behind the barn, sealed with a concrete slab poured in 1974, the year a nine-year-old named Zephyrine Marsh vanished from the farm. The fingerprints match hers. Gideon's POV; Zephyrine refuses to go near the field. The beat is the horror of a coincidence too perfect to be one.

chapters.title: Nineteen Seventy-Four
chapters.summary: In the county archive, Gideon finds the Marsh case file: a missing girl, a father who confessed to nothing, a search that ended at the well and stopped. A deputy's note says the family 'asked everyone to forget her.' His POV. The beat is the chill of institutional amnesia — a town that agreed not to remember.

chapters.title: The Thing in the Walls
chapters.summary: Night at the farmhouse: Gideon hears Zephyrine's own voice inside the plaster, calling to him in a register slightly wrong. The walls are full of fingerprints, hundreds deep, all hers, all decades old. His POV, terror escalating. The beat is realizing the house isn't haunted by her — it's holding her, and something else is wearing her voice.

chapters.title: Two of Her
chapters.summary: The thing in the walls takes Zephyrine's shape and stands in Ruth's kitchen asking to be let in. The real Zephyrine, waiting in the truck, tells Gideon the rule: only one of them can exist near the well. His POV, split between two identical faces. The beat is the cruelty of a choice that may already have been made.

chapters.title: Ruth's Bargain
chapters.summary: Ruth confesses: in 1974 her husband traded the girl to the well in exchange for the farm's survival through a ruinous drought — and the house has been collecting interest ever since. Her POV via a long, guilt-cracked monologue. The beat is the rotten arithmetic of survival: someone is always the payment.

chapters.title: Doors That Weren't There
chapters.summary: The farmhouse now has nineteen doors. Gideon opens one and steps into his own childhood kitchen, 1989, his mother calling him to dinner. He retreats, but Zephyrine lingers at the threshold, hungry for a past she never got to finish. His POV. The beat is grief disguised as architecture.

chapters.title: The Interest Comes Due
chapters.summary: Ruth is found standing in the cornfield, fingerprints covering her forearms, repeating Zephyrine's name. The house is calling in the debt, and it has begun taking the wrong person. Gideon's POV at the hospital, where Ruth's records show she was admitted in 1974 and never discharged. The beat is time folding in on its debtors.

chapters.title: Zephyrine's Confession
chapters.summary: Zephyrine admits she remembers everything: the well didn't take her, her father sold her, and she chose to stay rather than let the farm starve — a child's bargain, honored for fifty years. Her POV in a rare first-person chapter. The beat is the awful dignity of a sacrifice no one was allowed to remember.

chapters.title: The Other One Speaks
chapters.summary: The wall-thing negotiates through the radio: it will release Ruth and let the house die if the original is returned by the autumn equinox — six days. Gideon realizes it isn't a monster but the well's collector, bound like everything else. His POV. The beat is the unsettling sympathy of dealing with something that also just wants to be paid.

chapters.title: Six Days
chapters.summary: Gideon tries to find another way — lawyers, priests, a hydrologist to drain the aquifer — and every avenue dead-ends in 1974 paperwork that dissolves or names that don't exist. His POV, frantic and methodical. The beat is the claustrophobia of a problem with exactly one solution.

chapters.title: The House Remembers Me
chapters.summary: The farmhouse begins producing doors into Gideon's own memories, and one opens onto a summer afternoon where a small boy plays with a girl who was never imaginary. He watches himself at six, happy, and understands the house has been keeping his memories too — as collateral. His POV. The beat is heartbreak: his childhood was mortgaged.

chapters.title: What Return Means
chapters.summary: Zephyrine asks Gideon to promise that if she goes back, he won't dig her out, won't mourn her by name, won't keep her photograph — because remembrance feeds the well. He refuses, then sees what forgetting did to Ruth and understands. His POV. The beat is the terrible tenderness of agreeing to erase someone you love.

chapters.title: The Equinox Eve
chapters.summary: The house opens every door at once, a maze of borrowed rooms, and the wall-thing hunts them through Gideon's own past to stop the return — it would rather keep the girl than be paid. A running chase chapter, his POV. The beat is pure adrenaline: the past itself turned into a trap.

chapters.title: The Well Opens
chapters.summary: At the capped slab, Zephyrine breaks the concrete with her bare hands — the well has been waiting for its own — and the collector rises to take her early. Gideon fights it with the only weapon he has: the counted doors, the kept lights, the small order he imposes on haunted places. His POV. The beat is defiance against something vast.

chapters.title: Zephyrine Descends
chapters.summary: Zephyrine steps to the lip of the well, ages fifty years in fifty seconds as time takes back what it lent, and becomes an old woman, then a memory, then a warmth in the air. She thanks him for remembering her long enough to let her go. His POV. The beat is devastating release — the payment made in full.

chapters.title: The House Goes Quiet
chapters.summary: The doors close one by one until the farmhouse is only a farmhouse. Ruth wakes with no memory of a debt, a drought, or a girl. Gideon walks the empty rooms and finds the fingerprints fading like breath off glass. His POV. The beat is hollow victory — the silence you wanted, which is also the silence of her absence.

chapters.title: The Hole in the Shape of a Friend
chapters.summary: Weeks later, Gideon can't explain why he keeps a child's corduroy coat in his closet or why the name 'Zephyrine' makes his eyes sting. He drives past the Hollis farm and feels grief with no object. His POV, quiet and wounded. The beat is the price of survival: he kept his life and lost the reason he wanted it.

chapters.title: Eleven Doors
chapters.summary: On the last night of autumn, Gideon returns to the farmhouse, counts the doors — eleven, correct, ordinary — and finds one small handprint in the dust, fresh, placed deliberately where he'll see it. He doesn't wipe it away. Final chapter, his POV closing on an ambiguous grace note. The beat: some debts, once paid, leave a little change behind.
